title: Adding an AI agent to a Webflow site, and what it does to your speed scores
summary: Where an AI agent's script goes in Webflow, how it touches Core Web Vitals, and how to measure the speed cost on staging first. From Storylane.
body_markdown:
Before a Webflow team installs an AI agent, someone asks what it will do to the PageSpeed score. Then the argument starts. One person ran Lighthouse once and saw a drop. Another says the vendor promised it loads async. Nobody has a clean before and after, so the decision gets made on whoever sounds most sure.


I think the argument is the wrong shape. The speed cost of a website agent is mostly a placement decision you make inside Webflow, and you can measure it in an afternoon, on your staging subdomain, before a single real visitor sees it. I call it the twin-publish test: publish the same site to staging twice, once without the script and once with it, and compare the two the way you would compare any A/B result.


## Why does the speed argument about chat widgets never end?


The obvious explanation is that chat scripts are heavy and everyone knows it. Webflow's own guide to slow sites lists "third-party integrations" next to large images and excessive interactions as causes, and suggests updating, replacing or removing the ones that drag.


That explanation doesn't fully fit. The same script can be close to invisible on one site and noticeable on another, depending on where it sits in the page and when it does its work. So "chat widgets are slow" is too blunt to act on.


I have a theory for why teams stay stuck: both instruments they reach for are bad at before and after. Lighthouse lab scores move between runs of the same page. Google's Lighthouse documentation names ads, traffic routing, the test device and browser extensions as sources of that movement, and suggests treating performance "as a distribution of scores, rather than a single number." Field data has the opposite problem. PageSpeed Insights reports real Chrome users over the previous 28-day collection period, so the week you ship, the field numbers are still mostly about the site before the change. One noisy number and one slow number leave a gap, and opinion fills it.


The twin-publish test closes that gap: lab runs on staging, repeated enough to see the spread, then a field read once 28 days have passed.


## Where does the script go in Webflow?


Webflow gives you four places to put a third-party script by hand, plus a fifth route through apps. Everything below comes from Webflow's help center and developer docs, read on October 30, 2026.


Where Scope What Webflow's docs say about speed Use it for an agent when


Site settings, Custom code, Head code Every page "Adding external <script> tags to the <head> of your site can slow page loads." Webflow suggests the async or defer attribute. Only if the vendor requires it, and then with async or defer


Site settings, Custom code, Footer code Every page, placed before the closing body tag Scripts here let pages "load all their content before the JavaScript is processed, which helps with page load speed" You want the agent site-wide. This is my default


Page settings, Before </body> tag One page, placed after the site-wide code Same guidance: scripts before the closing body tag "typically" improve performance You want the agent on chosen pages only, such as pricing or product pages


Code Embed element Wherever you drop it in the design or a rich text field No separate speed guidance An inline experience, such as a full-page chat embedded in a section


An app using the Custom Code API Site or page, in the header or the footer Apps register scripts and apply them; changes only take effect when the site is published Your agent vendor ships a Webflow app rather than a snippet


Three practical notes from the same docs. Custom code needs a Core, Growth, Agency or Freelancer Workspace, or an active Site plan. Each custom code box takes up to 50,000 characters, which a loader snippet will never come near. And custom code runs in preview and comment modes but goes live only when you publish, which is exactly what makes the staging test possible.


The placement rule I'd follow: footer code, with the async attribute, unless you have a reason to do otherwise. It is the choice Webflow's own docs point to, and it is the one you should measure first.


## Which speed scores can a chat agent actually move?


Google's three Core Web Vitals each have a "good" threshold, read at the 75th percentile of page loads: Largest Contentful Paint within 2.5 seconds, Interaction to Next Paint of 200 milliseconds or less, and Cumulative Layout Shift of 0.1 or less. A chat agent touches each one through a different door, which is why one blanket score hides what is going on.


- **Largest Contentful Paint.** A script in the head that loads without async or defer can hold up rendering of the hero, which is often the element LCP measures. In the footer, or with async, the page paints first. If the launcher itself is large, check it isn't becoming the largest element.
- **Interaction to Next Paint.** This is where third-party JavaScript tends to show up, because any work the script does on the main thread competes with the visitor's first click or tap. In a lab run, look at Total Blocking Time and the third-party section of the Lighthouse report, which attributes main-thread time to each outside domain.
- **Cumulative Layout Shift.** A launcher that floats in a corner sits on top of the page. An embed that pushes content down as it appears can shift layout. If you embed inline, reserve its height in the Designer so nothing moves.


Put plainly: an agent's speed cost is decided by when its script runs, not by whether you have one.


## How do you run the twin-publish test on Webflow staging?


Webflow lets you publish to your staging subdomain (yoursite.webflow.io) without touching your custom domain, and its docs describe staging as useful "to test custom code" before you push live. That is the whole lab.


1. **Pick three templates.** The page with the heaviest hero, a CMS template such as a blog post, and the page where you most want the agent (often pricing). Templates matter more than individual pages, because every page built on one behaves alike.
2. **Publish the baseline to staging only.** In the publish menu, tick the webflow.io subdomain and untick your custom domain. If staging isn't hidden from search yet, turn off indexing for it in Site settings.
3. **Run each page five times on mobile** in PageSpeed Insights or Lighthouse, same device and network, extensions off. Record LCP, Total Blocking Time and CLS for each run, and keep the median and the spread. Five is my habit, not a rule from Google; the point is to see the distribution Google talks about.
4. **Add the agent's snippet to Footer code** with async, publish to staging only again, and repeat the same runs.
5. **Compare medians against the spread.** If the difference is smaller than the run-to-run movement in your baseline, you can't tell it apart from noise. If it is bigger, the third-party section of the report tells you how much main-thread time and transfer size came from the agent's domain.
6. **Try the alternatives you're unsure about.** Page-level placement only, or head with defer. One more staging publish each. This is where the test pays for itself, because you are choosing between placements with numbers rather than opinions.
7. **Ship, note the date, and read field data 28 days later.** PageSpeed Insights field data covers the previous 28 days, so a read before then still mixes old and new traffic.


Write down what change you'd accept before step 3, not after. A page sitting just inside a threshold has less room than one comfortably inside it, and deciding the budget after you see the numbers is how every result becomes "fine".


One more instrument Webflow offers: the site health scan, which checks settings such as minified HTML, CSS and JS and AsyncJS. Run it, but don't treat it as the answer here. Webflow's own FAQ says the scan doesn't cover everything and lists custom code among the things that can affect performance outside it.


## What about cookie consent?


Consent is the other question a webmaster gets asked, and it interacts with speed: if your consent tool holds scripts until a visitor chooses, the agent loads later for some visitors and not at all for others.


Webflow's consent guidance covers its own Analyze and Optimize tracking, and points to three routes: a consent management platform app or integration (it names DataGrail and Finsweet Components), connecting an existing platform such as OneTrust or TrustArc through Webflow's APIs, or building your own banner with custom code. Whichever you use, three steps belong in the install plan.


- Ask the vendor what the script stores in the browser, and decide with whoever owns privacy which consent category the agent falls into. This is a policy decision, not a speed one, and I won't pretend to make it for you.
- If the consent tool gates the agent, run the twin-publish test in both states: consent given and consent declined.
- Buyers ask about data handling too. We wrote up[what B2B buyers ask about AI website agents and data privacy](https://www.storylane.io/blog/ai-agents-data-privacy-b2b) , which is a useful list to have answers for before launch.


## Why put an agent on a fast site at all?


A webmaster who has spent a year shaving milliseconds is right to ask what the script is buying. My answer comes from our own data.


Across 10,580 buyer questions on 529 B2B websites, the Storylane Buyability Index found that 37.9% of fully answered questions were answered in the blog, help center or docs. The homepage supplied 1.8% of full answers and the pricing page 5.9%. Two caveats, every time: the questions are generated per company (what a buyer would plausibly ask), not logged from real buyers, and the 529 sites were chosen by the people who ran the scans, between September 8 and October 20, 2026.


The pattern is what matters for a webmaster. Most sites already have the answers. They sit several clicks from where buyers land, which we covered in[why B2B websites answer buyer questions in the docs, not on the homepage](https://www.storylane.io/blog/website-answers-hidden-in-docs) . A fast page that can't answer the question a buyer came with still loses them, just quickly (the same pipeline view we take on[bounce rate on a B2B website](https://www.storylane.io/blog/reduce-bounce-rate-b2b-website) ). An agent is a way to bring the docs answer to the page the buyer is already on, and that is the trade you are weighing against the milliseconds.


## How we run RepX on a Webflow site


I should be plain about my bias here: Storylane sells RepX, an AI sales agent for websites, and storylane.io runs on Webflow. So this is the setup I know best.


RepX comes in two forms, according to the[RepX launch guide](https://docs.storylane.io/repx-chat/setting-up-repx/launching-on-your-website) : a floating widget with a launcher in the bottom right or bottom center, and an immersive view embedded as an iframe for a dedicated page or for after a form is submitted. The embed code for both is in the RepX dashboard under Settings, Embed. On storylane.io, the RepX script tag loads with the async attribute (checked in our page source on October 30, 2026), which is the placement this article recommends.


For page-level control, RepX exposes JavaScript functions: *Repx.hide()* hides the launcher on a page, *Repx.open()* opens the chat panel, and *Repx.open("message")* opens it with a question already asked, so a button on your page can start a conversation. Qualified leads and conversation summaries flow to HubSpot, Salesforce and Slack. If you want the full setup sequence beyond the script, our guide to[deploying an AI sales agent on a B2B website](https://www.storylane.io/blog/build-ai-sales-agent) walks through it, and[page-level context for conversational AI](https://www.storylane.io/blog/page-level-context-conversational-ai) covers how the agent should behave differently by page.


Whatever agent you pick, run the twin-publish test on it. A vendor's word about async loading is a claim; two staging publishes and thirty Lighthouse runs are evidence.


## What to do on Monday


Before anyone argues about the agent's speed cost, publish your site to staging twice and measure. Put the script in Footer code with async, test three templates five runs each, write down your budget first, and read field data 28 days after launch. The speed question has an answer. It just takes an afternoon instead of a meeting.
